query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Degradation is primarily governed by the selective oxidation of titanium at the grain boundaries. In oxidizing environments, Ti preferentially forms a brittle TiO2 phase that depletes the matrix of critical strengthening elements, locally compromising the fcc structure and leading to embrittlement and fatigue degradation, while under reducing atmospheres, this oxidation is suppressed, preserving the alloy’s mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous fcc matrix and uniformly distributed elements.
generation.intervention: Expose identical alloy samples to controlled high-temperature tests under oxidizing (e.g., O2-rich) versus reducing (e.g., H2-diluted) gas environments.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposures (e.g., 800–1000°C) for extended durations (e.g., 100 hours), with one set in an oxidizing atmosphere and another in a reducing atmosphere, ensuring all other test parameters (heating/cooling rates, sample dimensions, etc.) are kept constant.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary regions where preferential oxidation of Ti leads to formation of a brittle TiO2-rich layer, causing local elemental depletion that undermines the cohesion of the fcc matrix.
generation.mechanism: In an oxidizing environment, Ti oxidizes preferentially, forming TiO2 at the grain boundaries. This local loss of Ti undermines the metastable fcc matrix, facilitating crack initiation and propagation (i.e., fatigue degradation). Conversely, in a reducing atmosphere the Ti oxidation is suppressed, maintaining the original composition and thereby the mechanical integrity of the alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, samples will exhibit significant TiO2 formation at grain boundaries, measurable Ti depletion in critical regions, and a notable decrease in mechanical performance (e.g., fatigue strength) relative to the as-built state. In reducing atmospheres, minimal oxide formation and negligible performance degradation are expected compared to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Performance measures and microstructural state of the as-built alloy without high-temperature gas exposure.
generation.boundary: Test conditions where temperature or gas composition are insufficient to drive significant oxidation (e.g., below 800°C or in atmospheres lacking oxidants) or conditions so extreme that additional degradation mechanisms (e.g., grain coarsening) dominate, making the selective oxidation effect indistinguishable.
generation.uncertainty: Without direct evidence from experiments on this specific composition and processing route, the contribution of Ti oxidation to degradation remains uncertain, and additional factors (e.g., oxidation of other elements, phase transformations) may also play significant roles.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical additively manufactured alloy samples. Expose one set to a controlled oxidizing gas environment (e.g., 21% O2 at 900°C) and the second set to a reducing atmosphere (e.g., diluted H2 in inert gas, also at 900°C) for 100 hours. Before and after exposure, conduct microstructural analysis (using SEM/TEM coupled with EDS) to quantify oxide formation and elemental distribution, particularly focusing on Ti at grain boundaries, and assess mechanical properties (e.g., fatigue testing).
measurements: Grain boundary oxide layer thickness and composition (via EDS and TEM)
Ti concentration profiles across grain boundaries (via EDS line scans)
Fatigue strength and crack-initiation behavior (mechanical testing)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If oxidizing environments do not result in significant TiO2 formation or observable Ti depletion at the grain boundaries – or if both oxidizing and reducing conditions yield comparable microstructural and mechanical properties – then the hypothesis that selective Ti oxidation governs degradation is falsified.
